strengths: The paper establishes a clean theoretical bridge between an information-theoretic quantity (class-conditional entropy production) and the statistical-physics speciation/symmetry-breaking instability of Biroli et al. (2024), deriving in closed form that the entropy transition occurs at the same logarithmic time scale t_s = (1/2) log d + O(1) for VP diffusion, with a rigorous asymptotic proof provided in the appendix (Sec. 4.3, App. A).

The analysis usefully distinguishes VP from VE/EDM kernels, showing the sharp O(1)-width transition collapses for VP but broadens as sqrt(d) for VE, a non-trivial and previously under-appreciated qualitative difference between commonly used SDE parameterizations.

The paper proposes a practical online posterior-tracking estimator (Algorithm 1) that allows the (partitioned) class-conditional entropy to be computed in trained, large-scale models without access to closed-form posteriors, and validates it on both EDM2-XS (ImageNet-512) and Stable Diffusion 1.5 (LAION-5B), which is a meaningful step from theory to an operational diagnostic.

The partitioned/hierarchical entropy construction is a sensible and creative device for resolving semantic decisions at different levels of abstraction (e.g., single-class vs. binary attribute partitions), and is demonstrated qualitatively on both class-level (ImageNet) and finer attribute-level (Stable Diffusion prompt variants) semantics.

The application to classifier-free guidance offers a novel and interpretable lens (Figure 3) connecting known empirical phenomena (e.g., limited-interval guidance improving FID, Kynkäänniemi et al. 2024) to a quantitative redistribution of entropy production across noise levels.

Limitations are discussed honestly, including reliance on calibration of the online posterior updates, the approximation used for the class complement, and an explicit failure case for Stable Diffusion (Figure 16, poor prompt adherence) rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result is derived only for isotropic Gaussian mixtures with equiprobable, high-dimensional-scaled components; while this matches prior theoretical work, it leaves open how much the qualitative alignment generalizes quantitatively to realistic, non-Gaussian, imbalanced class distributions such as ImageNet or LAION data.

The empirical validation on trained models (Sec. 5) is largely qualitative: entropy profiles and their overlap with denoised/generated samples are inspected visually (Figures 1, 3, 4, 6-16) without quantitative metrics that directly test the theoretical predictions (e.g., no measured transition widths, no comparison to predicted t_s, no statistical significance or confidence intervals on the estimated entropies).

The posterior-tracking estimator depends on an approximation of the class complement using the unconditional model (Appendix B), which the authors acknowledge can introduce bias 'when the proxy deviates from the true complement distribution,' but no sensitivity analysis or quantitative bound on this bias is provided.

The practical significance of the EDM/VE vs. VP distinction in the sharpness of the transition is explicitly left unresolved ('the practical significance of this difference is unclear... an interesting direction for future work'), which weakens the completeness of an otherwise central theoretical comparison.

The guidance analysis (Sec. 5.2, Figure 3) remains diagnostic rather than actionable: the paper shows that guidance redistributes entropy production but does not demonstrate that this signal can be used prospectively to design or improve guidance schedules (e.g., no closed-loop experiment showing the entropy-informed intervention improves FID/FD beyond existing heuristics).

Sample sizes for entropy estimation are relatively modest (300-3000 samples for ImageNet, 400 for Stable Diffusion) and no uncertainty quantification (e.g., confidence bands from finite-sample Monte Carlo estimation) is reported for the empirical entropy curves, which would be needed to assess estimator reliability.

Stable Diffusion 1.5 experiments are acknowledged to be limited by the model's poor prompt adherence and its limited ability to generate fine-grained detail, undermining the reliability of the fine-grained semantic analysis in this setting (Sec. 5.3, Appendix C.2).

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical derivation (Sec. 4, Appendix A) connecting the temporal derivative of class-conditional entropy to the Fisher divergence between class-conditional and marginal scores, and rigorously shows that for VP SDEs this entropy production concentrates on the O(log d) speciation time scale identified by Biroli et al. (2024), tying an information-theoretic quantity to the symmetry-breaking/speciation picture from statistical physics.

Introduces a partitioned (binary) version of the class-conditional entropy that is tractable to estimate online in trained models via a posterior-tracking procedure built on existing likelihood-ratio machinery, offering a practically computable diagnostic rather than a purely theoretical construct.

Includes non-trivial qualitative validation: entropy production peaks for specific ImageNet classes in EDM2-XS line up with visually inspected 'semantic emergence' in denoised trajectories, and similarly for text-attribute partitions in Stable Diffusion 1.5, with intuitive results (low-frequency attributes like color resolve earlier than high-frequency ones like object identity).

The analysis of how classifier-free guidance redistributes entropy production over the sampling trajectory (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 3) offers a plausible information-theoretic explanation for previously reported empirical phenomena regarding limited-interval guidance (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024).
weaknesses: Empirical validation on real models is narrow and largely qualitative/anecdotal: only three hand-picked ImageNet classes (tiger shark, eft, paintbrush) and a handful of hand-crafted prompt pairs for SD 1.5 are shown; there is no quantitative, large-scale test of whether predicted entropy-peak locations actually align with independently measured semantic emergence across many classes/prompts, so the central practical claim rests on a small set of illustrative examples.

There appears to be an unresolved tension between theory and experiments regarding the VP vs. VE/EDM forward processes: Section 4.3/Appendix A.2.3 proves that VE/EDM-type kernels do NOT exhibit a sharp O(1) transition (the mixing window broadens as sqrt(d)), yet the EDM2-XS experiments (which use an EDM/VE-like schedule) show clearly narrow, peaked entropy-production curves (Fig. 1b, Fig. 3). The paper does not clearly reconcile why the empirically observed sharpness for EDM2-XS matches the VP prediction rather than the VE prediction derived for the same kernel family, and explicitly states 'the practical significance of this difference is unclear,' leaving a core theoretical claim only loosely connected to the reported experiments.

The estimator relies on several ad hoc design choices acknowledged only briefly in Appendix B (fixing p(π)=0.5 regardless of the true partition prior to avoid degenerate reweighting, using the unconditional model as a proxy for the class complement, and using cross-entropy under guided trajectories as a proxy for entropy). These approximations are not validated against ground truth or analyzed for bias, so it is unclear how much the reported entropy profiles reflect genuine semantic dynamics versus estimator artifacts, particularly given the acknowledged out-of-distribution issues.

The paper does not demonstrate any new capability or improvement enabled by the proposed diagnostic (e.g., an improved guidance schedule, sampler, or training procedure); the guidance analysis in Sec. 5.2 largely re-describes previously known optimal guidance intervals (from Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024) through the entropy lens rather than showing that the diagnostic yields new, better interventions, which weakens the significance claim of providing 'a principled basis for time-localized control.'

For Stable Diffusion 1.5, the analysis is explicitly limited by poor prompt adherence, and the authors themselves show a failure case (Fig. 16) where the metric cannot be trusted because generated samples do not follow the intended prompt variant; this undermines confidence in the method's applicability to realistic text-to-image settings without substantial manual curation of prompts.

The theoretical model (equiprobable, isotropic, high-dimensional Gaussian mixture) is a considerable idealization relative to real deep generative models and hierarchical natural image data; while the hierarchical-branching discussion (Sec. 4.4) gestures at richer structure, no quantitative link is established between the idealized theory's predicted speciation time and the actual empirically observed peak locations in EDM2-XS/SD1.5, so the correspondence remains qualitative and somewhat asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical derivation connecting class-conditional entropy (and its temporal derivative) to the speciation/symmetry-breaking transition previously identified via SNR analysis (Biroli et al. 2024, Raya & Ambrogioni 2023), giving an information-theoretic operationalization of a physics-motivated phenomenon.

The asymptotic analysis for high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures is carried out carefully and explicitly for both VP and VE/EDM kernels, correctly showing the sharp O(1) transition exists for VP but not VE, which is a nontrivial and interesting distinction with derivations included in the appendix.

Introduces the useful notion of 'partitioned' class-conditional entropy restricted to binary partitions of the label/semantic space, which enables the method to resolve hierarchical/multi-scale semantic decisions (e.g., color vs. object identity) rather than being limited to a single coarse entropy curve.

The online posterior-tracking estimator (Algorithm 1) is a practical, model-agnostic technique that requires only the conditional and an unconditional/reference denoiser, and is validated on two realistic models/datasets (EDM2-XS/ImageNet and Stable Diffusion 1.5/LAION-5B), rather than only in toy settings.

The guidance-redistribution analysis (Figure 3) is a nice applied use-case, quantitatively showing how classifier-free guidance shifts entropy production toward higher noise levels and connecting this to prior empirical findings on limited-interval guidance (Kynkäänniemi et al. 2024).

The Stable Diffusion experiments with matched base/variant prompts (Figure 4 and Appendix C.2) provide an intuitive and visually corroborated demonstration that low-frequency/global attributes are resolved earlier (higher noise) than high-frequency/local ones, consistent with theory.

Limitations are discussed candidly, including reliance on calibration of the online posterior updates, the use of the unconditional model as a proxy for the class complement, and the poor prompt adherence of SD1.5 which complicates fine-grained attribute analysis (explicitly illustrated via a documented failure case in Appendix C.2).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are derived only for isotropic Gaussian-kernel forward processes and equiprobable, high-dimensional Gaussian mixture data; it is not established how tightly this stylized setting transfers to real, highly structured, non-Gaussian data manifolds beyond qualitative agreement in Figure 1/3/4.

The estimator's validity rests on an approximation (using the unconditional model as proxy for the class complement, Appendix B) whose bias is acknowledged but not quantified; no ablation or sensitivity analysis is given to show how estimation error affects the reported entropy peaks/locations.

Sample sizes used for entropy estimation are relatively modest (300-3000 samples for EDM2-XS, 200-400 for SD1.5) and no confidence intervals, variance analysis, or statistical significance tests accompany the entropy profiles or the guidance-redistortion results, making it hard to assess estimator noise versus genuine signal, especially for the more subtle SD1.5 curves.

The guidance-distortion analysis (Section 5.2) is demonstrated for only three ImageNet classes (tiger shark, eft, paintbrush), which is a very small and seemingly cherry-picked subset given ImageNet's 1000 classes; broader quantitative summary statistics across many/all classes would strengthen the generality claim.

The EDM/VE case explicitly lacks a sharp phase transition in the rescaled entropy (Figure 2b, Figure 5a), and the paper admits 'the practical significance of this difference is unclear,' leaving an important theoretical gap for one of the two major SDE families without resolution.

The paper's practical contribution is presented largely as a diagnostic/analysis tool; it does not propose or evaluate any new sampling, guidance, or training algorithm that leverages the entropy signal to improve generation quality or efficiency (e.g., no demonstration that entropy-based guidance-interval selection outperforms existing FID/FD-DINOv2-based selection), somewhat limiting the actionable impact claimed in the abstract ('provide a principled basis for time-localized control').

Stable Diffusion experiments are acknowledged to be confounded by poor prompt adherence (Figure 16 failure case), and the paper relies on manual verification of prompt fidelity rather than a systematic, automated filtering procedure, raising reproducibility concerns for that part of the evaluation.

strengths: Provides a rigorous, well-derived theoretical link between class-conditional entropy production and the 'speciation' transitions predicted by recent statistical-physics analyses of diffusion models (Biroli & Mézard, Achilli et al.), with explicit closed-form results for Gaussian mixtures under both VP and VE/EDM forward processes, including careful treatment of how the transition sharpens (VP) vs. broadens (VE) with dimension.

Extends the mechanism beyond Gaussian mixtures to the general 'Proper/Pure Density Decomposition' class-structure framework of Achilli et al. (2026), showing the same peak-at-speciation phenomenon holds more broadly (Appendix A.4), which strengthens the theoretical generality of the claim.

Translates the theory into a concrete, implementable estimator (Algorithm 1) for trained diffusion models, with a careful bias/robustness analysis (Appendix B: balanced priors, unconditional-model proxy, posterior-approximation error) that adds empirical credibility often missing in purely diagnostic papers.

Validates the method on both class-conditional (EDM2-XS/ImageNet) and text-conditional (Stable Diffusion 1.5 and, in the appendix, SDXL) models, across multiple classes and prompt families, showing consistent coarse-to-fine (low-frequency before high-frequency) semantic resolution patterns that align qualitatively with generated samples.

Applies the framework to analyze how classifier-free guidance redistributes semantic/entropy production over the trajectory, offering a novel quantitative lens on a previously mostly qualitative/heuristic phenomenon (limited-interval guidance effectiveness).

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed algorithmic description, hyperparameters, compute resources, and an extensive appendix with derivations and additional qualitative/quantitative experiments.
Limitations are discussed candidly, including estimator sensitivity to reference/complement model choice and prompt-adherence failure cases in SD1.5 (Figure 13), rather than being glossed over.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a diagnostic/analysis tool; it does not yield a new generation, guidance, or sampling algorithm that improves quantitative performance (e.g., FID/precision-recall) over existing baselines, so the claimed 'principled basis for control' is only partially realized and left largely as future work.

Much of the theoretical machinery builds directly on pre-existing frameworks (speciation theory from Achilli et al. 2026, posterior-estimation algorithm from Koulischer et al. 2025a), making the core novelty more of an integrative/analytical contribution than a fundamentally new method.

The trained-model experiments are relatively narrow in scope: EDM2-XS is a small model, and the highlighted quantitative analyses focus on only a few ImageNet classes and a handful of prompt families in SD1.5/SDXL; broader coverage across many classes/prompts or larger-scale production models is not systematically shown.

The estimator's practical validity depends on approximations (e.g., using the unconditional model as a stand-in for the true class complement, balanced priors) whose bias, while examined in synthetic Gaussian settings, is not thoroughly quantified in the more complex, high-dimensional real-model settings where ground truth is unavailable.

In the T2I setting, the diagnostic's reliability is confounded by model prompt-adherence quality, as explicitly shown by the SD 1.5 failure case (Figure 13), requiring manual curation of prompts, which limits turnkey applicability of the method.

No comparison to simpler alternative measures of semantic commitment (e.g., classifier confidence margins, other information-theoretic proxies) is provided to demonstrate that the proposed entropy-production diagnostic offers unique advantages over more straightforward heuristics.

strengths: Rigorous and largely self-contained theoretical derivation showing that class-conditional entropy production is governed by a pairwise posterior-competition/score-separation mechanism, worked out exactly for isotropic Gaussian mixtures under both VP and VE-EDM forward kernels (Section 4.2-4.3, Appendix A), and connected cleanly to the general speciation framework of Achilli et al. (2026).
The VP vs VE-EDM comparison (sharp O(1) transition window vs. broadened O(sqrt(d)) window) is a genuinely interesting and non-obvious theoretical observation (Figure 2, Table 1).

A practical online estimator (Algorithm 1) for the partitioned class-conditional entropy is proposed and its bias is carefully characterized through a decomposition into prior re-balancing, complement-model, and posterior-approximation error terms, validated on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and on EDM2-XS (Appendix B, Figures 7-8), which strengthens reproducibility.

Empirical results on EDM2-XS and Stable Diffusion 1.5/XL are reasonably thorough: class-specific speciation windows, a demonstration that guidance redistributes entropy production toward higher-noise stages, and a qualitative coarse-to-fine ordering of semantic attribute emergence replicated across several base prompts and an additional stronger model (SD XL).

The Limitations section and appendix failure-case analysis (e.g., poor prompt adherence in SD 1.5, Figure 13) are presented honestly rather than glossed over, which aids trust in the reported findings.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is largely a reformulation/instantiation of already-established speciation/symmetry-breaking phase-transition results (Biroli et al. 2024; Achilli et al. 2026) in an entropy-production language, rather than a qualitatively new phenomenon or mechanism; the main novel claim (entropy as an 'operational marker') is essentially a corollary of prior score-separation analyses, which limits originality.

Despite the abstract's claim of providing 'a principled basis for time-localized control,' the paper never actually proposes or tests a control/guidance algorithm that exploits the entropy signature; the guidance experiments (Section 5.2, Figure 3) are purely descriptive/diagnostic (showing that guidance shifts entropy production) without any downstream improvement in sample quality, efficiency, or controllability, so the 'actionable' framing oversells the contribution.

The estimator itself (Algorithm 1) is an adaptation of an existing posterior-update procedure (Koulischer et al., 2025a, Algorithm 2) rather than a new estimation technique, and its validity for realistic class structures (e.g., T2I prompts with unbounded/overlapping class sets) is explicitly flagged as approximate and untested beyond ImageNet-scale class sets and two mid-sized models (EDM2-XS, SD1.5), raising concerns about generality.

Key practical findings (e.g., the practical significance of the VP/VE transition-width difference, or why guidance-induced redistribution matters for downstream generation quality) are explicitly left as 'currently unclear' or 'an open problem for future work,' which weakens the paper's claimed significance.

The main-text experiments are somewhat narrow in scale (EDM2-XS and SD1.5, single-GPU scale models) with stronger/more relevant models (SDXL, SD3) relegated to a single appendix figure; combined with the acknowledged prompt-adherence confound in SD1.5 (Figure 13), the qualitative text-to-image claims about coarse-to-fine semantic ordering are not rigorously quantified (no statistics across many prompts, only a handful of qualitative examples).

Presentation relies heavily on the appendix (12+ pages of derivations and additional results) to support claims made compactly in the main text, making the main paper less self-contained and harder to independently verify without consulting ~20 pages of supplementary derivations.

strengths: Provides a clean, well-derived theoretical link between class-conditional entropy production and the symmetry-breaking/speciation transitions studied in recent statistical-physics analyses of diffusion models (Biroli & Mézard, Achilli et al.), extending the Gaussian-mixture analysis to both VP and VE/EDM forward processes and to the general 'proper/pure density decomposition' class-structure framework.

The theoretical derivation (Appendix A) is careful and self-contained: it derives the entropy-production identity from the Fokker-Planck equation, expresses it via pairwise score gaps and posterior log-odds, and rigorously shows (with explicit tail bounds) that the entropy production concentrates at the predicted speciation scale for VP and spreads over an O(sqrt(d)) window for VE, matching known results while adding new operational content.

Introduces 'partitioned' class-conditional entropy to resolve semantic decisions at different levels of abstraction (e.g., single class vs. complement, or binary attribute partitions), which is a useful and non-trivial generalization beyond the full K-ary entropy that is shown to reveal distinct speciation windows for different semantic attributes.

Validates the theory with a battery of experiments: synthetic Gaussian mixtures (1D and hierarchical, VP/VE, multiple dimensions) confirming the predicted scaling, and two realistic settings (EDM2-XS/ImageNet-512, Stable Diffusion 1.5/LAION-5B) where the online posterior-estimation algorithm is applied to real trained models.

Extensive robustness analysis in Appendix B (bias decomposition of the proposed estimator into prior-rebalancing, complement-model approximation, and posterior-approximation error, tested across dimensions and two Gaussian-mixture settings, plus convergence studies on EDM2-XS) substantially strengthens confidence in the practical estimator, which is often missing in similarly theory-heavy papers.

The guidance experiments (Figure 3, 12) provide a concrete, interpretable application of the diagnostic, showing how classifier-free guidance redistributes entropy production toward higher noise levels and connecting this to known guidance pathologies—this gives the theoretical machinery practical relevance beyond a descriptive statistic.

Limitations section is honest and specific (bias from using the unconditional model as a complement proxy, sensitivity to prompt adherence failures in SD1.5, need for stronger/better-aligned models), and failure cases are explicitly shown (Figure 13) rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The empirical validation on trained models is confined to one relatively small ImageNet model (EDM2-XS) and SD1.5 (with only a brief qualitative SDXL check in the appendix); claims about generality to practical, large-scale conditional models (e.g., strong T2I systems) remain largely untested, and the paper itself notes the T2I posterior-estimation approach degrades as the class set grows unboundedly.

The quantitative demonstration of the diagnostic's downstream utility is limited: the guidance analysis shows correlational redistribution of entropy production but does not use the diagnostic to produce an actionable improvement (e.g., a new entropy-informed guidance schedule that improves FID/FDDINOv2 beyond existing limited-interval guidance), so the 'principled basis for time-localized control' claimed in the abstract is only partially substantiated.

The posterior estimation procedure used in real models depends on several approximations (balanced partition priors, using the unconditional model as a proxy for the complement, finite-sample Monte Carlo and finite integration steps) whose bias is only characterized on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and on a small set of ImageNet classes; it is unclear how these biases behave in more complex, non-Gaussian, highly multimodal real data distributions beyond the limited empirical checks shown.

The qualitative SD1.5 attribute experiments (Figure 4, 13-18) rely on manually curated/verified prompts due to imperfect prompt adherence, which somewhat weakens the claim of a generally reliable diagnostic without human-in-the-loop curation, especially for weaker models.

The paper is dense and heavily notation-laden (many lemma-like derivations across main text and appendix); while rigorous, this could limit accessibility and reproducibility for readers who are not already familiar with the Achilli et al. and Biroli et al. formalisms, and some practical implementation choices (e.g., the specific 'reweighing priors' heuristic) are introduced somewhat ad hoc without a principled justification beyond empirical bias reduction.
